processing: An all-bud green tea shaped flat and straight during firing, so the buds stay whole and keep their silver down.
harvest_season: Single buds of spring; as is usual for bud-only Mengding teas, the earliest spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: Flat, straight, even single buds, fresh green and glossy under a full coat of silver down.
appearance_wet: Whole buds, tender green with a slight yellow cast.
taste_profile: A rich, tender-bud aroma and a mellow, fresh, savoury-sweet cup.

brewing.notes: Use a glass and cool water, as for other all-bud greens.

vintage_note: Sold as the current spring's harvest, and at its best within about a year, as with other tender Mengding greens. The earliest bud-only lots cost most. Mengding Shan Shihua is also protected as a geographical indication certification mark, so check the origin on the packet.
description:
Mengding Shihua, stone flower, is the flat, all-bud green tea of Mengding Mountain in Mingshan, near Ya'an in Sichuan. The modern tea carries one of the oldest famous names in Chinese tea.

Only single buds go in, and they are shaped flat and straight so each bud stays whole. The result looks almost silver because of the down, with fresh green showing through.

The fragrance is full and tender, and the cup is mellow and fresh more than bold. Buds this young scald easily, so go cooler than you would with a leafy green and watch the time.

It is sold by spring harvest, so ask the seller for the picking date. Taste it next to Mengding Ganlu and Huangya to see how three styles work from the same mountain.
history:
The name is old. The Tang-era Tang Guo Shi Bu ranks Mengding Shihua of Jiannan first among the empire's teas, and Mengshan tea went on being sent as tribute from the Tang through to the Qing.

The tea sold today is a modern recreation: the present flat, all-bud style dates to 1959. What the Tang tea looked like and how it was made is a separate question, so the shared name should not be taken as an unbroken recipe.
